To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the acquisition of a short-delay matching task was facilitated in children when they were required to emit a collateral behavior that was specific to the discriminative stimuli; (b) the acquisition of the same matching task was retarded in children when they emitted a collateral behavior that could occur regardless of the discriminative stimuli (i.e., was nonspecific in form to the discriminative stimulus); and (c) when emitting the same nonspecific collateral behavior the accuracy of children's matching was retarded by increasing
children who emitted sample-specific precurrent operants during a matching-to-sample task acquired matching more rapidly than did children who emitted precurrent operants of other types.

children who are trained to emit a collateral behavior that is specific in form to a discriminative stimulus will match to sample more accurately than children who are trained either to emit a collateral response that is not specific in form to the discriminative stimulus or to emit no collateral behavior.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects on human learning of precurrent behavior that occurs during the interstimulus interval of a short-delay matching task and is emitted by subjects prior to the onset of the comparison stimuli.
the role of precurrent operant behavior in the acquisition of a delayed matching-to-sample task.
the effects of a particular form of precurrent behavior on the acquisition and maintenance of a subsequent operant.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results accorded with the analysis of precurrent self-prompting behavior in children.
the present results are in accord with Skinner's analysis of precurrent responding.
the present results support Skinner's (1968) analysis and that they do not support the analysis of the precurrent behavior as "remembering".
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of precurrent behavior is not sufficient to produce the matching-to-sample response, but the presence of sample-specific precurrent behavior is.
precurrent self-prompting behavior is not a necessary but is a sufficient condition for the acquisition of short-term delayed matching-to-sample by children.
precurrent self-prompting of collateral behavior can facilitate the acquisition of a new operant, but can also interfere with its performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
collateral behavior can be used to promote memory performance in children.
collateral behavior can be a powerful determinant of matching performance.
children are able to engage in self-prompting behavior in the laboratory and that this behavior may be a useful adjunct to instruction in children who have difficulty learning.
